stances.question: Q01
stances.sideGloss: the machine executes laws imposed on it; reasoning stays with the human
stances.argument: Divides mathematical work into a mechanical part the engine can do and a reasoning part reserved for the intellect, because the machine is not a thinking being but an automaton acting by laws imposed on it.
stances.checked: Archive.org record for the French original (Bibliothèque universelle de Genève, n.s. 41, 1842); read the English translation at psychclassics.yorku.ca and found 'the machine is not a thinking being, but simply an automaton which acts according to the laws imposed upon it.'
stances.reviewNote: Menabrea states that the machine is not the being that thinks but executes the conceptions of the intelligence, which keeps all intellectual labour with the human.

stances.question: Q01
stances.sideGloss: the machine only executes what its operators order
stances.argument: The engine cannot originate anything; it can only do what we know how to order it to perform, and cannot anticipate analytical relations or truths.
stances.where: Notes by the Translator, Note G
stances.checked: Opened the York University 'Classics in the History of Psychology' transcription of the Notes and found the 'no pretensions whatever to originate anything' passage; publication in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs 3 (1843) stated there.
stances.reviewNote: This is Note G, where Lovelace says the engine has no pretensions to originate anything and can only do what we know how to order it to perform.

stances.question: Q01
stances.sideGloss: machines develop along their own line and may outgrow their makers
stances.argument: Machines are evolving far faster than animals and plants and may come to supplant humans as a new kind of mechanical life.
stances.where: Letter to the editor, The Press (Christchurch), 13 June 1863
stances.checked: Web search: Wikipedia and historyofinformation.com give the date, newspaper and pseudonym; the original is on Papers Past (not opened).

stances.question: Q01
stances.sideGloss: the machine works out what the premises contain; framing and interpretation are mental
stances.argument: Mechanism can replace most of the thought in logical deduction, but a mind must still frame the premises and interpret the machine's answer.
stances.checked: Archive.org record (Philosophical Transactions 160, 1870); read §54 in the OCR text: 'Mental agency is required only in interpreting correctly the grammatical structure of the premises'.
stances.reviewNote: The candidates cover the history of calculating aids and the mechanics of the keys; none reaches §54, where Jevons says a mind must frame the premises and interpret the result.

stances.question: Q01
stances.sideGloss: mind may evolve in machines beyond what was put in
stances.argument: An Erewhonian treatise argues that consciousness evolved from matter that showed no sign of it, so machines may likewise develop a new phase of mind their makers did not give them.
stances.where: Chapters XXIII–XXV, 'The Book of the Machines'
stances.checked: Opened Project Gutenberg #1906 table of contents and text; chapters XXIII 'The Book of the Machines', XXIV and XXV 'The Machines—continued/concluded' discuss mechanical consciousness.
stances.reviewNote: The treatise in 'The Book of the Machines' argues that consciousness arose from matter that showed none, so a new phase of mind may arise, and it points to the higher machines.

stances.question: Q01
stances.sideGloss: computers originate nothing
stances.argument: Quotes Lovelace to argue that electronic computers, like Babbage's engine, do only what they are ordered to do and should not be called electronic brains.
stances.checked: Web search: book based on Hartree's 1948 University of Illinois lectures, published 1949; IEEE Annals article on the Turing–Hartree dispute and Wikiquote record that he quotes Lovelace's 'no pretensions to originate anything'. Did not open the text.

stances.question: Q01
stances.sideGloss: a machine, especially a learning machine, can do what its maker did not supply
stances.argument: Answers 'Lady Lovelace's Objection' by noting that machines often surprise their makers and that a learning machine could produce things its programmer did not foresee.
stances.checked: Web search: Mind 59 (1950), 433–460; multiple sources confirm objection (6) is titled Lady Lovelace's Objection and Turing's reply. Not public domain; no link given.

stances.question: Q02
stances.sideGloss: a machine cannot converse appropriately, and that failure marks the absence of thought
stances.argument: A machine could utter words but could never arrange them to answer the sense of whatever is said to it, as the dullest human can; this shows it lacks reason.
stances.checked: Opened Project Gutenberg #59 (Veitch translation), Part V, and confirmed the two tests (use of words; reason as a universal instrument).
stances.reviewNote: Part V, in an English translation: Descartes's first test says a machine could emit words but never arrange them to reply to what is said, as the dullest men can.

stances.question: Q02
stances.sideGloss: appropriate, novel speech is the evidence of a mind in another body
stances.argument: I know other bodies have minds like mine because their speech is new, fitting and cannot be explained by mechanical principles alone.
stances.checked: Gallica record for the 1668 French text and archive.org record for the 1668 English translation found; argument summarized from the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Cordemoy. Did not read the text itself.
stances.reviewNote: Cordemoy says parrots and echoes do not speak because they only repeat, that to speak is to utter fitting words of one's own, and that bodies which answer his signs with fitting signs have souls; the 1668 English OCR is badly garbled and is kept as is.

stances.question: Q02
stances.sideGloss: in the materialist sense; speaking is a mechanical capacity, and a speaking creature would count as a thinking one
stances.argument: Proposes that an ape could be taught language by Amman's method for the deaf, after which it would be a little gentleman; speech is a trained bodily capacity, not proof of an immaterial soul.
stances.checked: Archive.org metadata for the 1912 Open Court French–English edition; search result from the archive.org full text confirms the ape-and-Amman passage. Imprint dated 1748, published late 1747.
stances.reviewNote: La Mettrie says Amman's method gave the deaf a soul and that a trained ape could learn a language and become a little gentleman fit for thinking.

stances.question: Q02
stances.sideGloss: fitting conversation can be scripted in advance
stances.argument: Edison's android Hadaly holds convincing conversations, but her speech plays from phonograph recordings written in advance by poets and philosophers, so her conversation shows other people's thought, not her own.
stances.where: Livre V, ch. I 'Première apparition de la Machine dans l'Humanité'
stances.checked: Opened Project Gutenberg #26681; Book V ch. I describes the two gold phonographs holding 'sept heures de ses paroles' composed by poets and metaphysicians.
stances.reviewNote: Edison explains that Hadaly's conversation plays from phonograph sheets written in advance by poets and metaphysicians, so she replaces an intelligence with theirs.

stances.question: Q02
stances.sideGloss: reasonable conversation could be built in without the machine reasoning
stances.argument: Answers Descartes by imagining a switchboard machine with a stored reply for every possible question; it could discuss any subject, but its maker would have done the thinking in advance.
stances.checked: Read the passage as quoted in Manuel Garrido, 'El autómata con discernimiento de Torres Quevedo', Límite 17 (2003) (Dialnet PDF), which gives the original venue as Revista de la Real Academia de Ciencias Exactas, Físicas y Naturales XII, 391–419. Did not open the original.

stances.question: Q02
stances.sideGloss: fitting output is not evidence of thought without feeling and self-awareness
stances.argument: A machine that produces sonnets or answers is not thinking unless it writes them from felt thoughts and emotions and knows that it has done so.
stances.checked: Web search: Lister Oration at the Royal College of Surgeons, published BMJ 25 June 1949; copy held in the Turing Digital Archive (AMT/B/44). Turing quotes it in 1950 as the argument from consciousness.

stances.question: Q02
stances.sideGloss: conversational performance is the appropriate test
stances.argument: Replaces 'Can machines think?' with the imitation game: a machine that converses indistinguishably from a human should be credited as we credit other people.
stances.checked: Web search: Mind 59 (1950), 433–460; sources confirm the imitation-game framing. Not public domain; no link given.

stances.question: Q03
stances.sideGloss: a machine can meet only situations its construction provides for
stances.argument: Machines act only from the disposition of their organs, which must be arranged for each particular action, while reason is a universal instrument usable in any circumstance.
stances.checked: Opened Project Gutenberg #59, Part V, and confirmed the 'universal instrument' passage.
stances.reviewNote: Part V, in an English translation: Descartes's second test says machines act only from the disposition of organs arranged for each action, while reason is a universal instrument for every occasion.

stances.question: Q03
stances.sideGloss: indeterminate situations require a mind
stances.argument: Calculation is determinate and can be mechanized, but in chess no move follows necessarily from the last and the opponent's will interrupts any fixed sequence, so a pure machine could not play.
stances.checked: Opened the Wikisource text; the passage beginning 'Arithmetical or algebraical calculations are, from their very nature, fixed and determinate' states the argument. Southern Literary Messenger, April 1836.
stances.reviewNote: Poe contrasts the determinate steps of calculation, which a mechanism can follow, with chess, where no move follows of necessity and the antagonist's will disrupts any fixed sequence.

stances.question: Q03
stances.sideGloss: the machine handles only cases foreseen in its cards
stances.argument: The engine cannot interpret a result that is not self-evident, such as a value becoming infinite; it can handle the case only if the programmer foresaw it and punched a card for it.
stances.checked: Read the English translation at psychclassics.yorku.ca: 'we should thus require of the machine to interpret a result not of itself evident, and that this is not amongst its attributes, since it is no thinking being.'
stances.reviewNote: Menabrea says that when a function passes through zero or infinity the machine rings a bell and stops for its attendant, unless the case was foreseen and cards were prepared for it.

stances.question: Q03
stances.sideGloss: a machine can respond to positions it was not given in advance
stances.argument: Every game of skill can be played by an automaton, because a machine that can choose the right move from any position of the pieces can answer whatever its opponent does.
stances.where: Chapter XXXIV, 'The Author's further Contributions to Human Knowledge' (section 'Games of skill can be played by an automaton')
stances.checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #57532; chapter XXXIV contains the side-note 'Games of skill can be played by an automaton' and the tit-tat-to discussion.
stances.reviewNote: Babbage reports his demonstration that every game of skill can be played by an automaton, since a machine that moves rightly from any position can answer whatever move its adversary makes.

stances.question: Q03
stances.sideGloss: an automaton can weigh circumstances and choose its action
stances.argument: The main object of automatics is automata with 'discernment' that take in impressions, weigh the circumstances and adapt their conduct as living beings do.
stances.checked: Read the passage as quoted in Manuel Garrido, 'El autómata con discernimiento de Torres Quevedo' (Dialnet PDF): 'que los autómatas tengan discernimiento ... adaptando su conducta a las circunstancias'. Did not open the original.

stances.question: Q03
stances.sideGloss: feedback machines adjust to conditions not fixed in advance
stances.argument: Machines governed by negative feedback correct their course toward a goal from information about their own errors, so purposeful behavior is not unique to organisms.
stances.checked: Web search: PhilPapers and SFI Press record the citation; several summaries confirm the feedback argument. Not public domain; no link given.

stances.question: Q03
stances.sideGloss: a learning machine can meet situations its programmer did not foresee
stances.argument: Proposes building a child machine that learns by reward and punishment, whose later behavior its teacher cannot fully predict.
stances.checked: Web search: Mind 59 (1950), 433–460; summaries confirm the learning-machine proposal. Section number not checked.

stances.question: Q04
stances.sideGloss: intention is only an occasional cause; God moves the body
stances.argument: There is no necessary connection between my will to move my arm and its motion; I do not know how to move it, so God is the true cause and my will only the occasion.
stances.where: Book VI, Part II, ch. III, 'Of the most dangerous Errour in the Philosophy of the Ancients'
stances.checked: Downloaded the archive.org OCR of Taylor's translation; ch. III of Book VI contains 'there is no necessary Connexion betwixt the Will we may have of moving our Arm ... and the Motion of the same Arm.' Published 1674–75.
stances.reviewNote: Malebranche argues that if the union of mind and body means God moves the spirits upon my desire to move my arm, then my arm is moved by God's will, not by my own impotent will; margin notes run into the OCR text of this English translation and are kept.

stances.question: Q04
stances.sideGloss: we cannot perceive whether or how intention causes action
stances.argument: We feel the arm move when we will it, but the power by which will produces motion is unknown and inconceivable; we observe only constant conjunction.
stances.where: Section VII, 'Of the Idea of Necessary Connexion', Part I
stances.checked: Project Gutenberg #9662 and davidhume.org confirm section titles; search excerpt quotes the 'unknown and inconceivable' passage. First published 1748 as Philosophical Essays concerning Human Understanding.
stances.reviewCheck: other: Hume accepts from experience that bodily motion follows the will; what he says we cannot perceive is the power or manner, not whether it does.
stances.reviewNote: Section VII, Part I: Hume says the motion of the body follows the command of the will, known only by experience, but the energy by which the will does this escapes all enquiry.

stances.question: Q04
stances.sideGloss: willed effort is directly known as a cause of movement
stances.argument: The primitive fact of consciousness is the feeling of willed effort meeting the body's resistance; in it we directly experience ourselves as a cause.
stances.checked: Downloaded archive.org Oeuvres inédites vol. 1 (ed. Naville, 1859) and found the 'effort voulu ... fait primitif' passage. Written c. 1812; first published in this 1859 edition.
stances.reviewNote: From 'Faits du sens intime', ch. IV rather than ch. I: Biran says we feel immediately that the will moves the body and is the cause of its movement, against occasionalism.

stances.question: Q04
stances.sideGloss: consciousness is an epiphenomenon
stances.argument: Neural events form a closed causal chain; states of consciousness are always conditioned by them and never condition them.
stances.checked: Archive.org record for vol. 1 (1870); Wikipedia and IEP credit Hodgson with the first modern statement of epiphenomenalism. Did not read the passage.
stances.reviewNote: Hodgson retracts his earlier view and says that if the nerve movements occurred without the pain and the idea of relief, the same muscular movements of pulling down the blind would follow.

stances.question: Q04
stances.sideGloss: conscious states do not cause bodily action
stances.argument: Consciousness is a collateral product of the body's working, like a steam whistle, and has no power to modify it; humans are conscious automata.
stances.where: Fortnightly Review 22 (1874), 555–580; reprinted in Collected Essays vol. I, Method and Results (1893)
stances.checked: Web search: Bodleian Archives, PhilPapers and IEP entry on epiphenomenalism give the citation and summarize the argument. No full text opened.
stances.reviewNote: The candidates come from other essays in the same Collected Essays volume (the 1870 essay on Descartes and 'The Progress of Science'), not the 1874 automata essay; none gives the steam-whistle or conscious-automata statement.

stances.question: Q04
stances.sideGloss: conscious states do not act on the body
stances.argument: Mind and body are strictly correlated and physical events have only physical causes, so feelings run alongside the nervous process without acting on it.
stances.checked: Web search gives the Fortnightly citation; archive.org record for Lectures and Essays (1901) where it is reprinted. Did not read the essay text.
stances.reviewNote: Clifford says physical and mental facts run in parallel without interference, that saying the will influences matter is nonsense, and that the body is an automatic machine; a running page header ('VOL. II D') sits inside the quotation and is kept.

stances.question: Q04
stances.sideGloss: will directs bodily and mental action
stances.argument: Much mental activity is automatic and physically caused, but the Will is an independent power that controls and directs that activity.
stances.checked: Archive.org record (1876 printing); 1874 Spectator reviews and summaries confirm the automatism-plus-Will position. Did not read the text.
stances.reviewNote: In the preface Carpenter holds both that automatic mental activity lies within physical causation and that an independent Will controls and directs it.

stances.question: Q04
stances.sideGloss: consciousness is efficacious
stances.argument: Consciousness is selective and grows more complex where the nervous system is least determinate, which would be useless if it had no effect; the automaton theory is an unwarranted a priori claim.
stances.where: Chapter V, 'The Automaton-Theory' (developed from 'Are We Automata?', Mind 4, 1879)
stances.checked: Archive.org record for vol. 1 (1890); Wikipedia and IEP confirm chapter V title; 'Are We Automata?' (Mind 1879, 1–22) is at psychclassics.yorku.ca/James/automata.htm.
stances.reviewNote: Chapter V: James calls the a priori automaton-theory an unwarrantable impertinence and argues that consciousness, growing more complex up the animal scale, must help the animal and so be efficacious.

stances.question: Q05
stances.sideGloss: human thought and conduct follow from bodily mechanism
stances.argument: The soul's faculties vary with the state of the brain, body, food and illness, so the whole person is a self-winding machine whose states follow from its organization.
stances.checked: Archive.org metadata for the 1912 Open Court French–English edition; Wikipedia entry confirms the work and dating (imprint 1748).
stances.reviewNote: In an English translation, La Mettrie argues from the mutual action of brain, blood and mind to the material unity of man, and says the will obeys the body a hundred times for each order it gives.

stances.question: Q05
stances.sideGloss: choices are necessary effects of physical causes
stances.argument: Man is part of nature and every act of will is determined by motives that act on the brain, so free agency is an illusion.
stances.where: Part I, ch. XI, 'Of the System of Man's Free Agency'
stances.checked: Web search confirms the chapter title in the Robinson translation on Project Gutenberg; archive.org record for an 1889 printing.
stances.reviewNote: In an English translation, d'Holbach says man is never a free agent: his passions, temperament and will follow necessarily from his physical composition and the motives acting on him.

stances.question: Q05
stances.sideGloss: mental life including will is explained by matter and force
stances.argument: There is no force without matter and no mind without brain; thought and will are functions of brain matter under natural law.
stances.checked: Archive.org records for German and English editions; did not open the free-will chapter, so no location given.
stances.reviewNote: In an English translation of a late edition, Büchner says spirit exists only on organized matter and that thought and feeling arise wherever matter is arranged and moved in a certain way in the brain; the passage does not mention the will.

stances.question: Q05
stances.sideGloss: mechanism excludes freedom, but the problem stays open
stances.argument: Under the mechanical view the brain's state at each moment is the necessary effect of the previous one, leaving no room for free will, yet the felt freedom of choice remains one of seven unsolved world-riddles.
stances.checked: Downloaded archive.org 1898 German edition of both lectures; read the passage 'dem Monismus ist die Welt ein Mechanismus, und in einem Mechanismus ist kein Platz für Willensfreiheit.' Lecture delivered 1880 to the Berlin Academy.
stances.reviewNote: Du Bois-Reymond sets out the mechanical view in which each brain state follows necessarily from the last, so monism leaves no room for free will; the passage gives this half of his position, not his claim that the riddle stays open.

stances.question: Q05
stances.sideGloss: free acts are not reducible to physical causation
stances.argument: Determinism treats conscious states as separate things in space; a free act comes from the whole self in real duration and cannot be predicted or explained by physical causes.
stances.where: Ch. III, 'The Organization of Conscious States: Free Will'
stances.checked: Project Gutenberg and archive.org records for the 1910 Pogson translation; Brock University Mead Project gives chapter III title.
stances.reviewNote: Chapter III in the English translation: Bergson says no reasoning will prove the psychic fact is fatally determined by molecular movement; the candidates do not reach his account of the free act as the expression of the whole self.

stances.question: Q05
stances.sideGloss: will is determined like any natural process
stances.argument: The struggle over free will has ended in favor of determinism; the human will is no freer than an animal's and differs only in degree.
stances.where: Ch. VII, 'Psychic Gradations' (section 'Freedom of the Will')
stances.checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #42968; ch. VII summary lists 'The Will—Freedom of the Will' and the text states the struggle 'has ended ... completely in favor of the determinist.'
stances.reviewNote: Chapter VII in the English translation: Haeckel says the struggle over free will has ended in favour of determinism and each act of will is fatally determined by organization and environment.

stances.question: Q05
stances.sideGloss: physics no longer shows choices to be fully determined
stances.argument: Quantum physics has withdrawn strict causality from the physical world, so physics no longer requires the complete determinism of mind that would rule out volition.
stances.checked: Downloaded the Gutenberg Canada HTML; ch. XIV 'Causation' has a section headed 'Volition' beginning 'From the philosophic point of view it is of deep interest to consider how this affects the freedom of the human mind'.
stances.reviewNote: In the 'Volition' section Eddington says that since physical laws are no longer strictly causal the materialist argument fails, and the choice among a brain's possible behaviours is volition.

stances.question: Q06
stances.sideGloss: necessity is compatible with, and needed for, responsibility
stances.argument: Actions are caused by character and motives like any natural event, and this necessity is what makes praise and blame possible; an uncaused act would reflect nothing about the person.
stances.checked: Project Gutenberg #9662 and davidhume.org confirm the section; search excerpt quotes its opening on necessary force in matter.
stances.reviewNote: Section VIII, §76: Hume argues that actions not caused by something durable in the person's character cannot make him answerable, so denying necessity would leave a criminal as pure as at birth.

stances.question: Q06
stances.sideGloss: responsibility requires freedom from necessity
stances.argument: Moral accountability requires a real power to will or not will an action; if every act were necessitated, no one would be responsible.
stances.where: Essay IV, 'Of the Liberty of Moral Agents'
stances.checked: Archive.org record (Edinburgh, 1788); IEP 'Thomas Reid: Theory of Action' gives Essay IV title and argument.
stances.reviewNote: Two candidates come from Essay V on moral judgment and the third rebuts arguments that liberty is impossible or hurtful; none states that accountability requires a power to will or not will.

stances.question: Q06
stances.sideGloss: people are not proper objects of blame for characters formed by circumstance
stances.argument: A person's character is formed for him by circumstances, not by him, so it is unjust for society to punish the characters its own arrangements produce; crime should be prevented, not punished.
stances.checked: Opened Yale Avalon Project text of the First Essay, which speaks of circumstances 'which inevitably form such characters as they afterwards deem it a duty and a right to punish'. First essay published 1813.
stances.reviewNote: First Essay: Owen says the few surround others with circumstances that inevitably form the characters they then punish, and that crimes should be prevented rather than punished.

stances.question: Q06
stances.sideGloss: causal determination does not remove responsibility
stances.argument: Human actions follow from character and circumstances, but 'necessity' is a misleading word; a person who can shape his own character and resist his habits is morally free.
stances.where: Book VI, ch. II, 'Of Liberty and Necessity'
stances.checked: Wikisource Book VI page and UT Austin transcription of ch. II found; search excerpt quotes Mill calling 'Necessity' an abuse of terms.
stances.reviewNote: Mill says a person is morally free who feels his habits are not his masters and could be resisted, and calls 'Necessity' an abuse of terms.

stances.question: Q06
stances.sideGloss: exposes how blame tracks bodily constitution arbitrarily
stances.argument: Satire of a country that tries and punishes people for illness and bodily failure, while treating forgery and violence as misfortunes of birth or upbringing needing cure.
stances.where: Chapters X 'Current Opinions' and XI 'Some Erewhonian Trials'
stances.checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #1906; ch. X opens with the trial of the sick and hospital care for criminals; ch. XI's judge addresses a defendant about his 'constitution'.
stances.reviewNote: The narrator's summary of Erewhonian law: illness is tried and punished, while forgery and violence are treated as misfortunes of birth or upbringing; the cut removes the grading of illnesses into crimes and misdemeanours.

stances.question: Q06
stances.sideGloss: moral responsibility; only social responsibility
stances.argument: Positivist psychology refutes free will, so punishment cannot rest on moral guilt; a person is held responsible only because he lives in society, and penalties are social defense.
stances.where: Part III, 'Positive Theory of Penal Responsibility', ch. I 'The Negation of the Free Will' and ch. IV
stances.checked: Downloaded archive.org 1917 translation; table of contents shows Part III ch. I 'The Negation of the Free Will' and ch. IV 'Man is responsible for his acts, because he lives in society'. Editorial preface dates first Italian edition to 1884.
stances.reviewNote: Ferri says juridical science can renounce subjective responsibility and calls social and objective accountability the more logical criterion; the passage opens mid-argument and 'the fact' refers to the defensive reaction described just before.

stances.question: Q06
stances.sideGloss: responsibility in the moral sense does not apply
stances.argument: Conduct follows from heredity and environment like the rest of animal life, so the legal idea of free will and personal guilt is a 'gross error' and punishment should give way to treatment.
stances.checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #12027; ch. III says 'the whole current conception of the individual and his responsibility is a gross error'.
stances.reviewNote: Darrow sets out the inherited idea of free will and personal guilt and then calls it a 'gross error'; the cut removes the example of an old indictment.

stances.question: Q07
stances.sideGloss: vital properties differ in kind from physical laws
stances.argument: Vital powers vary constantly in intensity while physical laws are fixed and uniform, so living bodies must be studied by different principles from inanimate ones.
stances.where: Part I, Article VII, §I 'Difference of vital powers with the physical laws'
stances.checked: Downloaded archive.org OCR of the 1809 Watkins translation; Article VII §I heading and text found. Archive.org also holds French editions (1805 and later). First edition 1800 (an VIII).
stances.reviewNote: Bichat's statement that vital powers vary constantly while physical laws are fixed, so the actions of life cannot be calculated like physical phenomena; OCR errors kept.

stances.question: Q07
stances.sideGloss: no vital force beyond physics and chemistry
stances.argument: Rejects a special vital force; living phenomena arise from the same kinds of forces as inorganic nature, arranged in complex ways.
stances.where: In Rudolph Wagner (ed.), Handwörterbuch der Physiologie, vol. 1
stances.checked: Web search: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on Wikisource and a Cairn.info chapter describe the article and its anti-vitalist argument. Did not open the text.

stances.question: Q07
stances.sideGloss: life requires a principle, identified with the soul
stances.argument: Defends animism: the vital principle is the same as the thinking soul, against both mechanist physiology and Montpellier vitalism's separate vital force.
stances.checked: Archive.org records for the 1862 edition; Gallica has the 2nd edition (1873); argument summarized from PhilArchive paper 'Reviving Spiritualism with Monads' and theses.fr record. Did not read the text.
stances.reviewNote: Bouillier describes the Montpellier vitalism of a separate vital force, says he will combat it, and states that animist vitalism, 'the only true one', makes the vital principle a power of the thinking soul; the cut removes a footnote that interrupts the sentence.

stances.question: Q07
stances.sideGloss: no separate force, but physics and chemistry do not account for the organization
stances.argument: Rejects vitalism because a vital force can do nothing except through physical and chemical forces, and rejects materialism because those conditions alone do not explain the ordering of vital phenomena.
stances.checked: Downloaded archive.org vol. 1 (1878); read 'Nous nous séparons des vitalistes, parce que la force vitale ... ne saurait rien faire par elle-même' and the matching passage on materialists.
stances.reviewNote: Bernard's explicit statement of both rejections: vital force can act only through general physical forces, and physico-chemical conditions cannot order vital phenomena; OCR errors kept.

stances.question: Q07
stances.sideGloss: life involves an impetus beyond physico-chemical process
stances.argument: Neither mechanism nor finalism explains evolution; life is a vital impetus that physics and chemistry do not capture, though he criticizes the older vital-principle theories.
stances.where: Ch. I, 'The Evolution of Life—Mechanism and Teleology' (section 'The vital impetus')
stances.checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #26163; table of contents and the passage on 'the stumbling-block of the vitalistic theories' checked.
stances.reviewNote: Bergson argues that the living being, marked by duration, differs from a mechanism and that the mechanistic conception can be refuted; this passage does not name the vital impetus itself.

stances.question: Q07
stances.sideGloss: life requires entelechy
stances.argument: An embryo fragment can form a whole organism, which no machine could do, so development requires a non-physical ordering factor he calls entelechy.
stances.where: Vol. 1, 'The Theory of the Harmonious-Equipotential System — First Proof of the Autonomy of Life' and ''Entelechy''
stances.checked: Downloaded archive.org text of vol. 1 (Gifford Lectures 1907); table of contents lists the sections quoted. Written in English.
stances.reviewCheck: other: the passage gives the second proof (an egg that remains whole through repeated division), not the embryo-fragment experiment the summary describes, though the argument is the same in kind.
stances.reviewNote: Driesch argues that no machine could be divided many times and remain whole, so development rests on entelechy; this is his second proof, from the egg's cell lineage, and the cut removes a methodological aside.

stances.question: Q07
stances.sideGloss: physical and chemical processes suffice
stances.argument: Life phenomena, including development and instinct, can be explained by physics and chemistry, and experimental control of them removes the need for a vital principle.
stances.checked: Archive.org records for the 1912 University of Chicago Press collection. Did not open the title essay.
stances.reviewNote: Loeb states his belief that even inner life is open to physico-chemical analysis and cites tropisms as instinct already explained on that basis.

stances.question: Q07
stances.sideGloss: mechanism fails, but no added vital force
stances.argument: The mechanistic theory cannot account for the way an organism maintains and reproduces its own structure, but vitalism is no better; biology needs the organism as its own basic concept.
stances.where: Lecture I, 'The Mechanistic Theory of Life' (on vitalism) and Lecture II, 'Criticism of the Mechanistic Theory'
stances.checked: Downloaded archive.org copy (Dutton, 1914 US edition); contents list four lectures; first published by John Murray, 1913.
stances.reviewNote: Haldane's own summary: objections to vitalism, the collapse of the mechanistic theory, and the organism as biology's working conception; the cut removes a sentence on the philosophy of physical concepts.

stances.question: Q08

stances.reviewNote: Spengler says the non-Western peoples learned the secret of Western technics and use it as a mere weapon against Faustian civilization, since it is no inner need for them; the ellipsis cuts a passage on the effects on white labour.

stances.question: Q34
stances.sideGloss: superior (industrial) nations have a right and duty to rule
stances.argument: The superior races have a right over the inferior races because they have a duty to civilize them; coaling stations are needed because a modern warship cannot cross the seas without them.
stances.checked: Wikipedia 'Jules Ferry' and Scribd copy date the speech 28 July 1885; the Latin Library excerpt (dated there to 28 March 1884) contains the 'superior races have a right because they have a duty' and coal-supply passages. The date discrepancy needs checking against the Journal officiel.
stances.reviewNote: Ferry states that the superior races have a right because they have a duty to civilize the inferior races; the passage grounds that right in race and civilizing duty, not in technology, and the coaling-station argument is not in the candidates.

stances.question: Q34
stances.argument: The tropics must be administered by the higher civilizations as a trust, because their resources are needed by the world and their peoples cannot develop them alone.
stances.checked: Internet Archive catalogue page (Macmillan, 1898); HathiTrust record; Spectator review of 20 August 1898.
stances.reviewNote: Kidd states that the tropics must be developed, that this can only happen under the white man, and that they can therefore 'only be governed as a trust for civilization'.

stances.question: Q34
stances.sideGloss: (satire); rule by firepower is mocked, not justified
stances.argument: Satirical verse whose narrator rests European mastery in Africa on the Maxim gun alone: 'Whatever happens, we have got / The Maxim gun, and they have not.'
stances.checked: WIST Quotations cites The Modern Traveller ch. 6 (1898); Google Books record; Wikipedia 'Maxim gun'.
stances.reviewNote: Belloc's narrator reports that Blood quelled the mutiny with 'We have got / The Maxim Gun, and they have not', then speaks piously of the duty to direct the native races, which the verse mocks.

stances.question: Q34
stances.sideGloss: superiority in weapons gives no right, only power
stances.argument: Technically superior Martians treat humans as Europeans treated the Tasmanians, and the narrator asks whether people who exterminated the Tasmanians can complain.
stances.where: Book I, Chapter 1, The Eve of the War
stances.checked: Project Gutenberg text; the Tasmanian passage is in Chapter 1 'The Eve of the War'.
stances.reviewNote: Wells's narrator compares the Martians' view of humans to human destruction of the bison, the dodo and the Tasmanians and asks whether we can complain if the Martians warred in the same spirit.

stances.question: Q34
stances.argument: Progress comes through struggle between races, and a scientifically efficient nation is justified in displacing less efficient peoples.
stances.checked: Internet Archive catalogue pages (address at Newcastle, 19 November 1900; Adam and Charles Black, 1901); Wellcome Collection record. Argument summary from secondary description, not a reading of the text.
stances.reviewNote: Pearson says progress follows inter-racial struggle, with a 'great civilization supplanting a lower race unable to work to the full the land and its resources'.

stances.question: Q34
stances.argument: Hobson rejects the claim that the struggle of races lets the 'socially efficient' justly govern or displace others, and traces imperialism to the interests of finance.
stances.where: Part II, Chapter II, The Scientific Defence of Imperialism
stances.checked: Marxists Internet Archive chapter page; Internet Archive catalogue page; Wikipedia entry.
stances.reviewNote: Hobson says biology and sociology supply 'thin convenient theories of a race struggle' so that financial and industrial interests can take the lands and labour of other peoples.

stances.question: Q34
stances.argument: Colonizers' claims of roads, railways and material progress do not justify colonial rule; the Congo-Ocean railway cost lives, and no one knows what these countries would have built without Europe.
stances.checked: Wikipedia (English and French) entries; auction and bookseller records of the first edition, Paris: Réclame, 1950.

stances.question: Q35
stances.sideGloss: for subjects; the artifice belongs to the sovereign
stances.argument: The commonwealth is an artificial man made by human art and could last as long as mankind if built by reason; but subjects who judge its laws by private conscience are a disease that dissolves it.
stances.where: Introduction; Chapter XXIX, Of those things that Weaken, or tend to the Dissolution of a Common-wealth
stances.checked: Wikisource Introduction page; Project Gutenberg text; chapter 29 title and opening confirmed via earlymoderntexts and Saylor copy.
stances.reviewNote: Hobbes says commonwealths could last as long as mankind if built by reason, but men as makers lack the art and humility to build them without 'a very able Architect'; the summary's point about private conscience is not in this candidate.

stances.question: Q35
stances.sideGloss: with limits; redesign must happen without halting the machine
stances.argument: The state may be rebuilt on reason, but unlike a clock it cannot be stopped for repair; the living clockwork of the state must be repaired while it runs.
stances.checked: Letter 3 text on monadnock.net contains the clockwork passage; Project Gutenberg Aesthetical and Philosophical Essays page.
stances.reviewNote: Schiller says a mechanic lets a watch run down to repair it, but 'the living watchworks of the state have to be repaired while they act'.

stances.question: Q35
stances.sideGloss: the state is not a machine
stances.argument: The state is not a machine or a factory but an organic union of all physical and spiritual needs grown through history, so it cannot be redesigned by contract.
stances.checked: Deutsches Textarchiv digitized 1809 edition; German Wikipedia entry on Adam Müller quoting the definition of the state.
stances.reviewNote: No candidate text was supplied for this work.

stances.question: Q35
stances.argument: The age trusts machinery in politics as in industry, believing good government is a matter of mechanical arrangements; Carlyle holds that social health depends on inward, dynamic forces that no constitution-making can supply.
stances.checked: Victorian Web pages on the essay (Edinburgh Review, June 1829); Internet Archive PDF listing.
stances.reviewNote: Carlyle says both parties treat government as a machine to be preserved or reconstructed and neglect the moral and spiritual condition of the people.

stances.question: Q35
stances.argument: Society is a growth and not a manufacture; constitutions are not made but grow, so treating the state as a contrivance to be redesigned mistakes its nature.
stances.checked: Econlib chapter text and Online Library of Liberty quote page; first published Westminster Review, January 1860.
stances.reviewNote: Spencer says the industrial organization grew without and against legislative guidance, as a seed becomes a tree; the phrase 'constitutions are not made but grow' is not in the candidates.

stances.question: Q35
stances.sideGloss: the machine must be broken and rebuilt
stances.argument: The state is a machine of class rule; the working class cannot simply take over the ready-made state machinery but must smash it and build a new one.
stances.checked: Marxists Internet Archive chapter pages (chapter 6 and section 'What Is To Replace the Smashed State Machine?'); Liberation School study guide. Written Aug-Sept 1917, published 1918.
stances.reviewNote: Lenin states that smashing the bureaucratic-military state machine and replacing it with something new is the real interest of workers and peasants.

stances.question: Q36
stances.sideGloss: within the office, no outside it
stances.argument: In the 'private' use of reason within an office, an officer, tax official or clergyman must obey and not argue; he may criticize freely only as a scholar addressing the public.
stances.checked: Marxists Internet Archive text; LibreTexts copy; published Berlinische Monatsschrift, December 1784.
stances.reviewNote: Kant defines the private use of reason in an office as passive obedience within a mechanism, while the same person may argue freely as a scholar before the public.

stances.question: Q36
stances.sideGloss: the official subordinates personal judgment to the universal
stances.argument: Civil servants are educated to a dispassionate, upright demeanor in which personal passions and ties give way to universal interests.
stances.checked: Marxists Internet Archive 'The State' section and UT Austin excerpt PDF quoting §294 and §296.
stances.reviewNote: Hegel says that in the great interests of a large state private ties and passions become powerless and officials acquire a habitual regard for universal interests.

stances.question: Q36
stances.argument: Most men serve the state 'not as men mainly, but as machines, with their bodies', as soldiers, jailers and constables, and so give up moral judgment; conscience must come first.
stances.checked: Opened Wikisource text from Aesthetic Papers (1849) and confirmed the 'as machines' passage.
stances.reviewNote: Thoreau's own statement that most men serve the state as machines, with their bodies, with no free exercise of moral judgment.

stances.question: Q36
stances.argument: Administration should be a separate science carried out by trained officials under political direction, kept apart from politics.
stances.checked: Internet Archive JSTOR early-journal item; Political Science Quarterly 2 (1887): 197-222; Wikipedia entry.
stances.reviewNote: Wilson states that administration lies outside the proper sphere of politics and belongs to the technical official; he does not address personal moral judgment directly.

stances.question: Q36
stances.argument: The state spreads each act of violence across many officials, each of whom says he only obeyed orders, so that no one feels responsible; every official must refuse.
stances.checked: Opened Marxists Internet Archive chapter 12 (responsibility diffused from soldier to Tsar); Project Gutenberg Garnett translation page; first published Germany 1894.
stances.reviewNote: Tolstoy describes how state organization divides responsibility for violence among so many hands that no one feels responsible; the call for each official to refuse is not in this passage.

stances.question: Q36
stances.argument: The honor of the civil servant is to carry out a superior's order conscientiously as if it were his own conviction, even when he thinks it wrong; personal responsibility belongs to the political leader.
stances.checked: Columbia-hosted translation text; Wikipedia entry; Max Weber Gesamtausgabe digital page. Lecture of 28 January 1919, Munich; published Duncker & Humblot 1919.
stances.reviewNote: Weber's statement that the official's honour lies in carrying out an order he thinks wrong as if it were his own conviction, while the leader bears personal responsibility.

stances.question: Q37
stances.sideGloss: the relation reverses, the body becomes part of the machine
stances.argument: In handicraft the worker uses a tool; in the factory the machine uses the worker, who becomes its living appendage.
stances.where: Chapter XV, Machinery and Modern Industry
stances.checked: Marxists Internet Archive chapter 15 page; quotations confirmed via Autodidact Project quote collection.
stances.reviewNote: Marx's direct statement that in the factory the machine makes use of the worker, who becomes its living appendage.

stances.question: Q37
stances.sideGloss: yes (the opponent), no (the main author)
stances.argument: An Erewhonian writer argues that machines are 'extra-corporeal limbs' and man a 'machinate mammal'; the Book's main author rejects this as a way of hiding the machines' growing independence.
stances.checked: Opened Marxists Internet Archive chapter 'The Book of the Machines (concluded)'; Project Gutenberg #1906 (1910 revised edition). Chapter numbers differ between editions.
stances.reviewCheck: other: the extra-corporeal-limbs argument is a separate Erewhonian writer's answer to the Book of the Machines; the candidates do not show the Book's author rejecting it as a way of hiding the machines' independence.
stances.reviewNote: The passage states the opponent's view (machines as extra-corporeal limbs, man a machinate mammal) in the narrator's report.

stances.question: Q37
stances.argument: Tools and machines are unconscious projections of the body's organs, with the hand as the model for all tools, so technology is the body carried outward.
stances.checked: Internet Archive catalogue page (Braunschweig: Westermann, 1877); HathiTrust record; Meiner edition page describing Organprojektion.
stances.reviewNote: Kapp states that the hand shaped tools after itself and that organ and mechanism relate as model and copy, which he calls organ projection.

stances.question: Q37
stances.sideGloss: the tool is defined by not being an organ
stances.argument: Instinct uses organized instruments that are part of the body, while intelligence makes inorganic tools that stay separate from it and can be varied without limit; this separateness defines homo faber.
stances.checked: French Wikisource page image of the 1907 edition; secondary summaries of chapter II; Project Gutenberg page for Mitchell translation.
stances.reviewCheck: other: Bergson also calls the made instrument 'an artificial organ by which the natural organism is extended', so the tool's separateness from the body is not absolute in this passage.
stances.reviewNote: Bergson contrasts instinct's organized instruments, part of the body, with intelligence's unorganized instruments that can take any form.

stances.question: Q37
stances.argument: Anything that takes part in the conscious movement of the body is added to the body schema; a woman's sense of location may extend to the feather in her hat.
stances.checked: Brain 34 (1911): 102-254, Oxford Academic record and Zenodo record; feather quotation from Wikipedia 'Body schema' and Vallar 2025 review.
stances.reviewNote: The only candidate is website boilerplate with no text from the work.

stances.question: Q37
stances.argument: The blind man's cane stops being an object in his hand and becomes an extension of his bodily reach; habit incorporates the tool into the body schema.
stances.checked: Wikipedia entry; secondary accounts (PhilArchive paper) of the blind man's stick example.

stances.question: Q38
stances.sideGloss: tools replace rather than add to capability
stances.argument: The savage's body is his only instrument and is stronger for it; had he an axe, a sling or a horse he would lose the strength and speed he now has.
stances.checked: Oxford Text Archive and Marxists Internet Archive texts of the First Part; axe/sling/ladder/horse passage confirmed.
stances.reviewNote: Rousseau's own passage that the body is the savage's only instrument and that hatchet, sling, ladder or horse would cost him his strength and speed.

stances.question: Q38
stances.argument: Man is weak in himself but a tool-using animal: 'without Tools he is nothing, with Tools he is all.'
stances.where: Book I, Chapter V, The World in Clothes
stances.checked: Opened Wikisource chapter and confirmed the quotation. Serialized in Fraser's Magazine 1833-34; first book edition 1836 (Boston).
stances.reviewNote: Teufelsdröckh's 'without Tools he is nothing, with Tools he is all', with the editor's endorsement of the definition.

stances.question: Q38
stances.argument: 'The civilized man has built a coach, but has lost the use of his feet'; each gain in equipment is a loss of the person's own strength and skill.
stances.checked: Dartmouth-hosted text and Emerson Central; quotation confirmed.
stances.reviewNote: Emerson's passage that society gains arts and loses instincts, including 'The civilized man has built a coach, but has lost the use of his feet.'

stances.question: Q38
stances.argument: 'Men have become the tools of their tools': the farmer and the householder serve the equipment that was meant to serve them.
stances.checked: Quote Investigator and Digital Thoreau text of 'Economy'.
stances.reviewNote: Thoreau says the farmer's house has got him rather than he the house; the phrase 'tools of their tools' is not in the candidates.

stances.question: Q38
stances.argument: People are strong by borrowing the might of the elements; steam, gravity and electricity do their work, so a person should 'hitch his wagon to a star'.
stances.checked: Project Gutenberg Society and Solitude; Michigan Emerson complete works text; quotations confirmed.
stances.reviewNote: Emerson says a man should hitch his wagon to a star and that we are strong by borrowing the might of the elements.

stances.question: Q38
stances.sideGloss: with reservations
stances.argument: With his auxiliary organs man has become 'a kind of prosthetic God', but the organs have not grown onto him, give him trouble, and have not made him happy.
stances.checked: Projekt Gutenberg-DE chapter 3 page; English quotations from Stephen Hicks PDF of the text and Wikipedia.
stances.reviewNote: Freud says man has become a god by means of artificial limbs that do not grow on him and still give trouble, and is not happy with it (this translation says 'artificial limbs', not 'prosthetic God').

stances.question: Q39
stances.argument: Pygmalion loves the ivory statue he made, knowing it is his own work, and Venus rewards that love by bringing it to life.
stances.checked: Wikisource translation page for the Pygmalion episode.
stances.reviewCheck: other: the text also says Pygmalion 'does not own it to be ivory', so his love partly denies its artificial nature, though his prayer shows he knows it is ivory.
stances.reviewNote: The prayer and animation scene: Pygmalion knows the statue is ivory and Venus grants his wish.

stances.argument: The sculptor knows Galathée is marble and his own creation and loves her anyway; the play treats that love as sincere and grants it.
stances.checked: Wikipedia entry (written 1762, first performed Lyon 1770); Internet Archive catalogue page for an early edition.
stances.reviewNote: Pygmalion says he knows it is marble and his work yet loves the figure; the OCR is badly garbled and the translation marks doubtful readings.

stances.question: Q39
stances.argument: Nathanael loves the automaton Olimpia while he believes she is alive; when he sees she is a mechanism his love turns to madness and he dies.
stances.checked: Wikipedia and Staatsbibliothek Berlin Hoffmann portal; Project Gutenberg listing for Bealby's Weird Tales vol. 1.
stances.reviewNote: The scene where Spalanzani reveals Olimpia as an automaton and Nathanael falls into madness.

stances.question: Q39
stances.argument: Lord Ewald, told by Edison exactly how the android Hadaly is made, accepts her in place of the real woman he could not love.
stances.checked: Project Gutenberg #26681 (French text); Gallica record; Wikipedia and SF Encyclopedia entries.
stances.reviewCheck: other: Ewald accepts Hadaly, but in the same scene says he hopes to forget what Edison told him of her mechanism, which qualifies 'told exactly how she is made'.
stances.reviewNote: Lord Ewald accepts the android after Edison's explanations and says he is eager to be the prisoner of this enigma.

stances.question: Q39
stances.sideGloss: such love is self-love
stances.argument: Nathanael's love for Olimpia is narcissistic: he forgets his real fiancée for a doll that reflects his own complex back to him.
stances.checked: Opened Project Gutenberg German text (Imago, 1919); passages on Olimpia and narcissistic love confirmed.
stances.reviewNote: Freud calls Nathaniel's love for Olimpia narcissistic and says it estranges him from the real love object.

stances.question: Q39
stances.argument: A man marries the household robot he helped build and lives with her until death, and the story presents the marriage as real love.
stances.checked: Wikipedia entry: Astounding Science Fiction, December 1938.

stances.question: Q40
stances.sideGloss: a machine cannot take part in conversation
stances.argument: A machine might utter words in response to a touch, but it could never arrange words to answer the meaning of whatever is said to it, as even the dullest person can.
stances.checked: Wikisource Part 5 page; Adelaide eBooks text. Bears on companionship only indirectly.
stances.reviewNote: Descartes's first test: a machine may emit words on being touched but cannot arrange them to reply to what is said, as the dullest men can.

stances.question: Q40
stances.sideGloss: (satire)
stances.argument: Satire in which Prince Oronaro prefers a doll stuffed with sentimental novels to the real queen; the play mocks a love that needs nothing back.
stances.checked: German Wikipedia entry (premiered Weimar, 30 January 1778); Projekt Gutenberg-DE text page.
stances.reviewNote: The only candidate is the website's front matter and cast list, with no text stating the position.

stances.question: Q40
stances.argument: Nathanael feels only Olimpia understands him though she answers only 'Ah, ah'; the story treats this companionship as delusion.
stances.checked: Project Gutenberg listing; plot summaries. The 'Ah, ah' detail is from the story but was not re-read for this entry.
stances.reviewNote: Olimpia's only words are 'Ach! Ach!', yet Nathanael says only she understands him; the narrator notes she never uttered other words.

stances.question: Q40
stances.argument: Edison argues that the android Hadaly, with recorded speech and no inner life of her own, will be better company for Ewald than the shallow woman she copies.
stances.checked: Project Gutenberg #26681; plot summaries (SF Encyclopedia, Wikipedia). Whether Hadaly lacks feelings is contested within the novel.
stances.reviewNote: Ewald fears being alone with the 'unconscious Eve' and Edison replies he will be less alone than with her model.

stances.question: Q40
stances.argument: The child's doll takes all the love given it and answers with silence, because it is made of stuff that cannot respond; Rilke treats this as the child's first experience of not being loved back.
stances.checked: Zeno.org and Projekt Gutenberg-DE texts (the 'schwieg' passage); first published Die weißen Blätter, 1914. Argument summary based on the silence passage.
stances.reviewNote: Rilke says the doll answered our love with silence because it was made of worthless stuff, and that this may leave some suspecting they cannot be loved.
